newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's documenta art show sums up the century.
newsitem.headline: Germany's documenta art show sums up the century.

text.p: documenta X, Germany's leading international art exhibition, opens on Saturday as a rarefied, cerebral multimedia fair that tries to drink in the past, the future and the complexity of today's world.
Staged roughly every five years since 1955, documenta aims to live up to its self-proclaimed status as the "world's most important exhibition of contemporary art".

This year's model, under the artistic direction of 42-year-old Frenchwoman Catherine David, strives to integrate the Internet, film, theatre and travel diaries as well as more traditional visual arts.

A concerted effort was made to include Latin Americans and Africans as well as Europeans and North Americans among the 250 artists, who address pressing social issues such as the move of Germany's capital to Berlin and Israeli-Palestinian relations as well as well as more detached, formal themes.
"I don't know what is meant by the visual arts, classical arts," David told a news conference on Thursday.

The show has made a landmark of the central city of Kassel, near the former border between east and west Germany, and over the years it has helped to highlight the history of the Cold War and the fall of communism.

The overtly political but sometimes opaque current show addresses that past by reprising works of artists such as Walker Evans and Jean-Luc Godard, while looking ahead with pieces by rising young stars.
"The last documenta of the century can hardly avoid the task of reflecting on its own history," said David, whose brash, curt style has made her a lightning rod for criticism in the art world.
Tempers flared at thee news conference over the last-minute removal of a work by Belgian artist Marcel Broodthaers.

documenta has been intimately tied with Joseph Beuys, Germany's most prominent postwar artist, who died in 1987, but who bequeathed the city a green and growing monument in the form of his work "7000 Oaks".
Not confined to traditional gallery settings, the works pervade the city, in the old City Hall, the train station, underground pedestrian walkways and in the open air.
One work deals with the denazification of city planning in the reconstruction of Kassel after World War Two.
The sponsors, including Deutsche Bahn AG, Sony, the Sparkassen Group, IBM Deutschland and Volkswagen AG, hope attendance will surpass the 615,000 visitors who came to documenta IX in 1992.

Historians, philosophers, architects from around the world -- and even a neurophysiologist -- will hold 100 lectures, one for each day of the exhibition which runs through September 28, to make the documenta experience different for all visitors.

"Here one can investigate the prospects for the future, even if they are uncomfortable or irritating," said Christian Hohmann Denhardt, minister for science and culture for the state of Hesse. "The aim of art is not to please at any price. We are sure the spark of artistic friction will catch fire."
